anime.def: Japanese shortening of animēshon, from English “animation”. It came into everyday use in the 1970s. Before that people said dōga or manga eiga (cartoon films), and TV anime was often called terebi manga.

manga.def: Comics, and the source of a large share of anime. The word was popularised by Hokusai's sketchbooks (1814 onward), where it meant something like “whimsical pictures”.

doga.def: Literally “moving picture”. The older Japanese word for animation (as in Tōei Dōga), and also the studio term for in-between drawings.

genga.def: Key animation: the drawings at the important poses of a movement. Key animators are credited individually, and fans follow their work.

nakawari.def: The drawings that fill the gaps between key drawings. Usually made by junior animators, and often outsourced.

sakuga.def: Drawing, or the quality of the drawing and animation. Among fans it means a standout sequence of animation, celebrated for the individual animator who made it.

cel.def: A clear celluloid (later acetate) sheet. Characters were traced and painted on cels, which were laid over painted backgrounds and photographed. Japanese TV stopped using them in 2013.

bank.def: A library of finished footage reused across episodes: a robot launching, a weapon firing, a magical girl transforming. Cheap to repeat, and repetition turned it into ritual.

kuchipaku.def: Lip flap. Mouths are drawn on separate layers in a few shapes and swapped over a held face, so dialogue costs very few drawings.

tome.def: A single drawing kept on screen for a stretch of time, often with a camera move across it. The basic tool of limited animation.

ova.jp: オリジナル・ビデオ・アニメ
ova.def: Original video animation: made for sale on tape or disc rather than for TV or cinema. The first was Dallos (1983). OVAs gave niche and adult stories a market.

seiyu.def: Voice actor. In Japan a recognised profession with its own stars, concerts and fan culture.

otaku.def: A devoted fan. Popularised as a mocking label by the columnist Akio Nakamori in 1983, stigmatised after a 1989 murder case, and slowly reclaimed from the 2000s.

moe.def: Literally “budding”. A protective, affectionate attachment to fictional characters, and the designs built to provoke it.

mecha.def: Robots and machines, and the genre built around them. “Super robots” (Mazinger Z) are near-mythic; “real robots” (Gundam) are mass-produced weapons.

shonen.def: “Boys”. A marketing category (from manga magazines such as Weekly Shōnen Jump), not a genre: action, sport, comedy and romance all appear in it.

shojo.def: “Girls”. A marketing category whose manga, from the 1970s on, developed much of the medium's language of feeling and inner life.

seinen.def: Works aimed at adult men, often from magazines such as Young Magazine (where Akira ran).

isekai.def: “Other world”. Stories in which someone is transported or reborn into a fantasy world. A dominant genre of the 2010s, much of it adapted from web novels.

iyashikei.def: “Healing type”. Gentle, low-conflict works meant to soothe, such as Mushishi or Aria.

sekaikei.def: “World type”. Stories in which a teenage relationship is tied directly to the fate of the world, with society in between left out. Usually traced to Evangelion.

spokon.def: Sports plus konjō (guts): stories of training, suffering and will, such as Star of the Giants and Tomorrow's Joe.

mahoshojo.def: A genre of girls with magical powers, from Sally the Witch (1966) to Sailor Moon (1992) and its deconstruction in Madoka Magica (2011).

henshin.def: Transformation: the sequence in which a hero or magical girl changes into their powered form. Usually bank footage.

mediamix.def: Telling one story and selling one character across manga, TV, film, toys, games and merchandise at once. Scholar Marc Steinberg traces it to Astro Boy's chocolate-sticker campaign of 1963.

seisakuiinkai.def: A group of companies (publisher, broadcaster, toy maker, music label, distributor) that jointly fund an anime and split its rights. It spreads risk; the studio that makes the show often owns none of it.

simulcast.def: Streaming an episode abroad, subtitled, within hours of its Japanese broadcast. Standard since the 2010s.

ma.def: The interval between things: a pause, an emptiness left on purpose. Hayao Miyazaki used the word for the quiet moments in his films.

mononoaware.def: A classical Japanese term for a gentle sadness at the passing of things, such as falling cherry blossoms.

emaki.def: Illustrated hand scrolls, read right to left an arm's width at a time. The golden age of the form was the 12th and 13th centuries.

kamishibai.def: “Paper theatre”: a storyteller slides illustrated boards through a small wooden frame. Popular with children from about 1930 to the 1950s; several manga artists started in it.

utsushie.def: An Edo-period magic lantern show in which performers moved hand-held wooden projectors behind a paper screen, so painted images walked, flew and transformed.

benshi.def: Live narrators who stood beside the screen during silent films, voicing characters and explaining the story. Often more famous than the films.

harmony.def: A frame in which the character is painted in the textured style of the background, freezing a key moment like an illustration. Osamu Dezaki made it his signature; fans call these frames “postcard memories”.

itano.def: Swarms of missiles corkscrewing through the frame on smoke trails, as animated by Ichirō Itano for Macross (1982) and much imitated since.

seichi.def: “Pilgrimage to sacred places”: fans travelling to the real locations behind a work's backgrounds, such as Washinomiya Shrine (Lucky Star) or the stairs in Your Name.

satsuei.def: Literally “photography”. Once the filming of cels; now the digital department that layers drawings, backgrounds and effects and adds light, blur and atmosphere.

mukokuseki.def: “Stateless”. Characters and settings without clear ethnic or national markers. Scholar Kōichi Iwabuchi argued that this “culturally odourless” quality helped anime travel.
